  • Show global tags: display labels shared by all users for sorting object information

  • Show tag labels: display additional labels on objects

  • Show global service templates: display ready-made maintenance schemes available to all users

  • Show object tree tooltips: enable pop-up tooltips when you hover over objects in the list

• Show LRS radius: display the coordinate accuracy radius when the device determines its location by LBS (cell towers)

  • Group markers on the map: combine closely located objects into groups, making the map more readable

  • Marker animation: add movement to icons on the map

  • Full-screen map: display the map at full screen

How to set up:

  • In the “Personalization” tab, find the “Settings” section

2. In this section you will see a list of options

3. To enable an option, select its checkbox

4. After selecting the options you need, click the “Save settings” button in the “Personalization” tab

Tooltips

In the “Tooltip elements” section you can choose what additional information is displayed when you hover the cursor over an object icon on the map.

How to set up:

  • In the “Personalization” tab, find the “Tooltip elements” and “Additional tooltip elements” sections

  • Select the elements you need by selecting the checkbox in the required field

3. Click “Save settings” in the “Personalization” tab

Measurement system

Here you can configure:

1. The measurement system:

  • Metric: kilograms, liters, kilometers

  • Imperial: pounds, gallons, miles

    2. The number format

    3. The first day of the week for the calendar and reports

How to set up:

  • In the “Personalization” tab, find the “Measurement system” section

  • Select the options you need from the drop-down lists

  • Click “Save settings” in the “Personalization” tab

Now all data will be displayed in a format convenient for you, and the calendar and reports will match your work schedule.
karta-i-geokoding:
Here you can configure:

— address display

— display of events on the map

— color indication of speed

Address display

You can configure which address components are visible in the system, for example in reports or in pop-up windows on the map.

  • Hide the address if there is a geofence: the system shows only the geofence name if the address is inside it

  • Reverse address order: display the address in reverse order, from the country to the house number

How to set up:

  • In the “Map and geocoding” tab, find the “Address display settings” section

2. In this section you will see a list of address components

3. To enable a component, select its checkbox

4. After selecting the settings you need, click the “Save settings” button in the “Map and geocoding” tab

Displaying events on the map

In the “Display of events on the map” section you can configure which event types are displayed in the object's history.

When you go to the “Events” tab in the “History” section, you will see the list of events you selected for display.

The places where these events occurred are also marked on the map with markers. For example, you see “Parking” events in the list and select a record you are interested in. When you click the event record, the exact place where it was recorded appears on the map.

How to set up:

  • In the “Map and geocoding” tab, find the “Display of events on the map” section

  • Select the event type to display in the object's history by selecting the checkbox in the required field

  • Click “Save settings” in the “Map and geocoding” tab

    This way, in the “Display of events on the map” section you can select event types and then view them in the list and on the map in the “History” section.

Color indication of speed

Color indication of speed shows speed changes in different colors. On the track in the movement history, you will see how fast the object was moving at each moment.

How to set up:

  • In the “Map and geocoding” tab, go to the “Speed in color” section

    2. Select the checkbox next to the “Speed in color” function to display the track in the history in color.

Color indication of speed is already set up in the system by default:

Gray: the vehicle is stationary

Green: slow driving, up to 60 km/h

Yellow: medium speed, up to 90 km/h

Red: fast driving, over 90 km/h

If you want to change the color of the standard indication:

  • Double-click the color field you want to change

    2. Select the color you need from the list

3. Click the “Update” button

4. Click the “Save” button in the “Speed in color” section

If you want to add a new color field:

  • Click the button for adding a new color

2. In the new field, select a color and set the speed

3. Click the “Save” button

To delete a color field, click the icon next to it.
spisok-otchyetov-1:
In the “Report list” tab you choose which report types you want to use. The types selected here will be available when you create a new report.

How to set up:

  • Go to the “Report list” tab

  • Select the report types by selecting the checkbox next to the report name you need

3. Click the “Save settings” button

The selected report types are displayed the same way in both the web version and the mobile app.

To learn how to work with reports and configure them, see the “Reports” section.
nastrojki-kml:
KML/KMZ is a special file that lets you put additional geographic data on the map:

— points

— lines

— areas

— images

This file works like an additional transparent layer that can be overlaid on the main map. Such a layer helps display the information you need: mark important objects, show boundaries, or plot a route.

The main map stays visible, and the additional information is overlaid on top.

You can upload a KML/KMZ file to PILOT and see the additional geographic data on the map.

Where to get a KML/KMZ file:

1. Create one yourself:

  • In Google Earth

  • Edit a text document manually

    2. Download ready-made files:

  • From specialized sites with geographic data

  • From open map databases

  • From specialized communities and forums

How to upload a file to PILOT:

  • Go to the “KML settings” tab

2. In the “KML/KMZ upload” section, select the data source for uploading

“URL”: if the file is on the internet

“File”: if the file is on your computer

3. Add a link to the file or select the file on your computer

4. Enter the file name that will be displayed in PILOT

5. Click the “Save KML/KMZ” button

If you want all users of the contract to see the file, select the “For all” checkbox.

To delete an uploaded KML, click next to it.

After a KML file is uploaded, the “Object layers” tool appears on the map.

How to display layers on the map:

1. Find the “Object layers” panel: a list with checkboxes for selection. It is located in the upper right part of the map

2. Expand the list and select the checkboxes next to the layers you need. You can select one or several layers at the same time

3. The selected layers are displayed on the map, and the main map stays visible.
tegi-obektov:
An object tag is a short label with information that helps you quickly understand what an object is. Think of a tag as a name sticker for each object.

The sticker displays information:

  • A short name

  • A color code

  • A description

    In the tag information you can specify, for example, the type of object, its role, or its state.

Tags are needed to:

— quickly find the object you need

— tell one object from another

— track and group objects

— organize objects in the list

How to add object tags:

  • Go to the “Object tags” tab in the contract settings

2. Click the “Add label” button

  1. In the window that opens, fill in the tag information:

  • Come up with a name

  • Choose a color

  • Write a short description

  • Select with checkboxes the objects that will have the label

4. Click the “Save” button

If you want a tag to appear automatically when a new object is created, set it as a “Default” tag.  In this case, when you create a new object, this tag will be present in the tags field automatically. You won't have to add this tag to the object card manually.

After you fill in the tag information, a record for it appears in the “Object tags” tab.

This is how objects with tags look in the list. When you view the object list, in the “Labels” column you will see color markers that correspond to the objects' tags.

You can add several tags to one object to describe it by different criteria.
personal-i-gruppy:
In the “Staff and groups” tab you can create employee accounts and configure their access to PILOT. For each user you can define the available objects, reports, modules, and actions in the system.

This section describes:

— creating and editing users

— configuring the user card

— assigning access rights

— creating and applying rights templates

— searching for users

— viewing login history

— assigning available reports

— setting up IP filtering

— blocking and unblocking accounts

The available settings depend on the connected modules and the rights of the current user.

An administrator can create users and manage their access.
sozdanie-polzovatelya-1:
Users can be created and configured by an administrator. When creating an account, enter the login details, and then define which objects, tags, modules, and actions will be available to the employee.

How to create a user

1. Open “Contract settings” and go to the “Staff and groups” tab

2. Click the “Add user” button in the upper right corner

3. In the card that opens, fill in the user data on the “Settings” tab

Required fields are outlined in red:

  • Login: the name the user will enter to log in to PILOT

  • Password: the password for logging in. Click the edit icon in the field to set the password

  • Name: the employee's name or another clear name for the account

  • Type: the user's access level. PILOT has two user types:

  • Administrator: can add users and objects, work with drivers, and manage the rights of the contract's users

  • User: works only with the objects, data, and functions assigned to them. The available capabilities are determined by their rights

  • Email: the e-mail address. Click the send icon in the field to send the user an e-mail with a link to log in to PILOT

  • Mobile phone: the employee's contact number

  • Information: additional details about the user. Fill in this field if necessary

    4. Click “Save”

The created account appears in the list in the “Staff and groups” tab.

After creating the user, open their card and configure access on the corresponding tabs. Depending on the connected modules, you can assign here:

— vehicles

— drivers

— object tags

— rights to view and change data

— access to modules

— interface parameters

— other available functions

The set of tabs depends on the contract configuration and the administrator's rights.

How to edit a user

1. Open the “Staff and groups” tab

2. Find the user in the list

3. Double-click the user's row

4. Make changes in their card

5. Click “Save”

How to delete a user

Find the user in the “Staff and groups” tab and click the trash icon in their row.

After deletion, the user loses access to PILOT. Before deleting, make sure the account is no longer needed.

The account owner and the user you are currently logged in as cannot be deleted in the PILOT interface. This restriction protects the account from losing access.

The account owner is highlighted in green in the list.

If you need to delete the owner, first assign another contract owner in the admin panel. After the owner is changed, deletion becomes available.

If you don't have access to the admin panel, contact the administrator or technical support.
kartochka-polzovatelya:
The user card configures the employee's credentials and rights in PILOT. Here you can define which objects, drivers, tags, reports, and modules will be available to them, and which actions they can perform.

The card may contain the following tabs:

  • Settings: login, password, contact details, user type, and additional account parameters

  • Climate chambers: access to the modes, objects, and data of the “Climate” module

  • Vehicles: selecting the objects the user can view and use

  • Drivers: selecting the drivers available to the user

  • Object tags: assigning the tags the user can use to find and filter objects

  • Rights: permissions to view, create, change, and delete data, as well as access to individual functions and modules

  • Interface: configuring the available sections and interface elements

  • “Situation center” event groups: access to event groups and “Situation center” functions

The set of tabs depends on the connected modules, the contract configuration, and the rights of the user who performs the configuration. Therefore user cards in different accounts may differ.
nastrojki-polzovatelya:
The “Settings” tab specifies the account data, login parameters, and the history period available to the user.

Main settings

Fill in the user data. Required fields are outlined in red:

  • Login: the name the user enters to log in to PILOT

  • Password: the password for logging in. To create or change it, click the edit icon in the field

  • Name: the employee's name or another clear name for the account

  • Type: determines the access level:

  • Administrator: can add users and objects, work with drivers, and manage the rights of the contract's users

  • User: works with the objects and functions assigned to them. The available capabilities are determined by their rights

  • Information: additional details about the employee. Fill in this field if necessary

  • Email: the e-mail address. Click the send icon in the field to send the user an e-mail with a link to log in to PILOT

  • Mobile phone: the employee's contact number

Additional settings

  • Number of login attempts (The number of possible login attempts): specify the allowed number of authorization attempts. The parameter limits repeated login attempts with incorrect credentials. A value of 0 turns off attempt counting.

  • Number of days to store history: specify the period for which historical data is available to the user, including when building reports:

  • 0: use the standard period of 365 days

  • a positive number: keep history for the specified number of days

  • −1: do not keep history

The maximum period is determined by the contract configuration Users default parameters. It is added by a user with access to the admin panel. If you need to increase the available period, contact the administrator or technical support.

For example, a value of 730 in the max_days_available_history parameter lets you give the contract's users access to two years of history. After the configuration is applied, the “Number of days to store history” field is filled in with the set number of days.

After filling in the fields, click “Save”. Then go to the other tabs of the card to assign objects, tags, and the necessary access rights to the user.
klimaticheskie-kamery:
The “Climate chambers” tab configures the user's access to the data of the “Climate” module. You can grant access to the whole mode or only to individual objects and sites.

The module has two modes:

  • NORMAL (Standard): the standard mode for working with climate sensors. It shows connected objects and sensors, their current readings, update time, and charts

  • VELAVU: a mode for equipment, sites, and premises loaded from the Velavu platform. In this mode you can view the structure of sites, buildings, and floors, as well as the location of devices and RFID tags on the map or plan.

To grant access:

1. Open the user's card

2. Go to the “Climate chambers” tab

3. Select the checkbox next to the mode you need

  • NORMAL: access to the module's standard data

  • VELAVU: access to the Velavu integration data

4. To grant access only to individual data, expand the mode you need and select the checkboxes next to the corresponding elements:

  • in NORMAL mode: groups or objects with climate sensors

  • in VELAVU mode: sites, buildings, or individual floors

5. Click “Save”
transport-1:
The “Vehicles” tab configures the user's access to monitored objects. The user will see in PILOT only the objects selected here.

To grant access:

1. Open the user's card

2. Go to the “Vehicles” tab

3. Expand the folder you need

4. Select the checkboxes next to the objects that should be available to the user. To select all objects in a folder, select the checkbox next to its name

5. Click “Save”.

New objects are not assigned to users automatically. After creating or importing an object, open the cards of the users you need and grant them access manually. This also applies to objects received from a mapping contract.

voditeli-1:

1. Open the user's card

2. Go to the “Drivers” tab

3. Expand the group you need

4. Select the checkboxes next to the drivers available to the user. To select the whole group, select the checkbox next to its name

5. Click “Save”

tegi-obekta:
The “Object tags” tab configures the user's access to tags used to classify and quickly search for objects. The user will be able to see and use only the selected tags.

To grant access:

1. Open the user's card

2. Go to the “Object tags” tab

3. Select the checkboxes next to the tags you need

4. Click “Save”

To close access to a tag, clear the corresponding checkbox and save the changes.
prava:
The “Rights” tab configures the actions the user can perform in PILOT. For example, you can allow them to view reports and edit objects but forbid creating or deleting data.

Rights are combined into thematic groups. The set depends on the connected modules and the account configuration. Here there may be permissions for:

— working with vehicles

— creating and editing objects

— managing sensors and tags

— viewing and building reports

— working with geofences

— access to financial data

— changing contract settings

— using additional modules

Configuring rights

To grant rights to a user:

1. Open the user's card

2. Go to the “Rights” tab

3. Expand the group you need

4. Select the checkboxes next to the allowed actions

5. Click “Save”

The checkbox next to a group enables all the rights nested in it. If the user needs only certain capabilities, expand the group and select them manually.

To find the right you need faster, enter its name in the search field.

Grant only the rights the employee needs for work. Access to objects, drivers, and tags is configured separately in the corresponding tabs of the card.

Rights templates

A template saves a configured set of rights and helps you quickly assign the same permissions to several users. For example, you can create the templates “Dispatcher”, “Manager”, or “Reports specialist”.

How to create a template

1. Open the card of a user with a suitable set of rights

2. Go to the “Rights” tab

3. Click the save template icon

4. In the “Saving a template” window, enter a clear name

5. Click “Save”

The template appears in the list of saved templates. To open this list, click the icon in the “Rights” tab.

In the list you can view and delete templates you no longer need.

How to apply a template

To assign saved rights to another user:

1. Create a user or open their card

2. On the “Settings” tab, expand the “Type” field

3. Select the option marked “(template)”

4. Fill in the rest of the user's data

5. Click “Save”

The selected set of rights will be applied to the user.
gruppy-sobytij-situatsionnogo-tsentra:
The “Situation center event groups” tab (Control Room event groups) configures which event groups are available to the user when working with the “Situation center” module.

The event groups themselves are created and configured for the whole contract in “Contract settings”, in the “Control Room” (“Situation center”) tab. In the user's card you can only grant or close access to groups that already exist.

2. Go to the “Situation center event groups” tab

4. Click “Save”

rfid-metki-1:

komandy:

interfejs:
The “Interface” tab configures which sections and modules are displayed to the user. If the checkbox is selected, the corresponding element is available in the interface. If you clear the checkbox, the element is hidden.

Example: hiding the object tree

The Online Tree parameter controls the display of the object tree in the “Online” tab.

To hide the object tree:

2. Go to the “Interface” tab

Object tree enabled

poisk-polzovatelya:
In the “Staff and groups” tab you can find a user by login, account name, or e-mail address.

1. Enter part of the value in the search field in the upper right corner

2. The list updates automatically and shows only matching records

You can type your query in uppercase or lowercase letters; case does not affect the search results.

To show all users again, clear the field with the icon .

Account owner

istoriya-vkhodov:

naznachenie-otchyetov:
For each user you can choose the reports that will be available to them in PILOT.

1. Open the “Staff and groups” tab

2. Find the user you need

3. Click the report list icon in their row

4. In the “User rights to reports” window, select the checkboxes next to the reports you need

5. Click “Save”

ip-filtratsiya-dlya-polzovatelya:
IP filtering restricts account login by IP address. After you enable it, the user can log in to PILOT only from allowed addresses.

To set up IP filtering:

1. In the “Staff and groups” tab, find the user you need

2. Click the filter icon next to their name

5. Click “Save IP list”

blokirovka-i-razblokirovka-polzovatelya:
Blocking temporarily prevents a user from logging in to PILOT but keeps their account and access settings. In the “Status” column, the user's state is indicated by color:

green icon: the user is active

red icon: the user is blocked

How to block a user

1. In the “Staff and groups” tab, find the user you need

2. Click the green icon in the “Status” column

3. In the confirmation window, click “Yes”

The status changes to red . After blocking, the user cannot log in to PILOT

How to unblock a user

1. Find the blocked user in the list

2. Click the red icon in the “Status” column

3. In the confirmation window, click “Yes”

The status changes to green, and the user can log in to the system again with their previous credentials.
planirovshchik-otchyetov:
The report scheduler is a tool for generating and sending reports automatically on a schedule.

With the scheduler you can:

— select the report type

— set the period whose data is included in the report

— specify the time and frequency of report generation

— select objects or tags

— specify the e-mail addresses the report is sent to

To use the report scheduler, confirm your e-mail address on the “Privacy” tab.

How to create a schedule

1. Open the “Report scheduler” tab

2. Click “Add new schedule”

3. In the window that opens, configure the report parameters, the data period, and the generation schedule

4. Select the objects or tags to generate the report for

5. Click “Save”

The schedule is then created, and reports are generated and sent at the specified frequency.

Report parameters

In the “Report parameters” block, fill in the following fields:

  • Name — enter a descriptive name for the schedule

  • Language — select the language of the generated report

  • Report type — select a report from the list. The list shows only the report types you have access to. You can view the available reports on the “Report list” tab

  • Sensor groups (Select tags) — select the sensor tags whose data should be included in the report. Tags let you generate a report only for the sensors you need. You can assign tags in the sensor settings. The availability of the field and the list of tags depend on the selected report type.

  • Grouping — specify how to group data in the report, for example by dates or by objects

  • Breakdown — select the intervals the data in the report is split into, for example by day, by week, or with no additional breakdown

If you select a report type that supports maps, additional settings appear in the scheduler. Which settings appear depends on the selected report:

  • Show maps (Show maps) — adds a static map with the object's route for the report period to the report.

  • Map type (Map Type) — lets you select the base map used in the report, for example OSM or Google Sat. The selected base map is used when the “Map type” (Show maps) option is enabled

  • Show parking — marks parking locations on the map with P icons. This option is available only after “Show maps” (Show maps) is enabled

  • Show odometer (Show odometer) — adds odometer readings at the start and end of the trip to the table, if the selected report supports this option

These settings are saved in the schedule and applied every time the report is generated automatically.

  • Report time zone — select the time zone used to determine the data period and the time of events in the report

  • Format — select the file format: PDF or Excel

  • Page size — select the page size, for example A4

  • Orientation — select the page layout: “Portrait” (vertical) or “Landscape” (horizontal). For reports with many columns, select “Landscape” to fit the table to the page width.

  • Emails — specify one or more e-mail addresses to send the report to. To remove an address from the list, click the cross next to it.

Make sure your e-mail address is confirmed on the “Privacy” tab. You cannot use the report scheduler without a confirmed address.

Recipients can unsubscribe from a specific report using the link in the e-mail. If no recipients remain in the list, PILOT suspends report generation. The schedule is kept. After you add a new recipient, sending resumes from the current period.

Report data period

In the “Report data period” block, set the time interval whose data should be included in the report.

  • From — specify the time from which data is included in the report

  • Previous day — enable this option if the start time of the period belongs to the previous day

  • To — specify the time up to which data is included in the report

  • Period — select the duration of the period

The “Previous day” option lets you generate reports for intervals that start on one day and end on another.

For example, if you specify:

  • period start — 20:00

  • enable “Previous day”

  • period end — 08:00

the report will include data from 20:00 of the previous day to 08:00 of the current day.

Generation schedule

In the “Generation schedule” block, specify when and how often the report should be created.

  • Next generation — select the date and time of the nearest report generation and sending

  • Frequency (Generate) — specify how often the report should be generated:

  • daily — the report is generated every day

  • weekly — the report is generated once a week

  • monthly — the report is generated once a month

  • selected days — the report is generated only on the specified days of the week

Below the schedule settings, the “Data period” is displayed — the automatically calculated interval whose data will be included in the next report.

Selecting objects or tags

On the right side of the window, select the objects to generate the report for:

  • “Objects” — the report is generated for the selected objects

  • “Tags” — the report is generated for the objects grouped by the selected tags

You can select individual objects or an entire group of objects. Use the search bar and filters for quick search.

Saving the schedule

Before saving, check the schedule settings and click “Save”.

Unsubscribing from a scheduled report

You can stop receiving a scheduled report using the link in the e-mail. You do not need to sign in to PILOT to unsubscribe.

Unsubscribing applies only to the report and e-mail address shown on the confirmation page. Other scheduled reports will continue to arrive. The other recipients of this report keep their subscription.

How to unsubscribe

1. Open the e-mail with the scheduled report

2. Click the “Unsubscribe from this scheduled report” link

3. On the page that opens, check the report name and e-mail address

4. Click the “Unsubscribe” button

PILOT removes the specified address from the recipient list and shows a message confirming a successful unsubscription, with the report name.

If you are already signed in to PILOT, following the link and unsubscribing keep your current session.

How to unsubscribe

A token is a unique access code that lets other users see the location of objects without having access to your account.

Put simply, a token is like a temporary pass. It gives limited access to specific information without revealing your personal data or password.

On the “Tokens” tab you can create two types of tokens:

  • Monitor token — for viewing the location of selected objects via a public link

  • Access token — for signing in to PILOT without entering a password

View token (Monitor token)

A Monitor token gives another person access to a map with the selected objects and their movements. The recipient of the link does not get a login, a password, or full access to the account.

Rights to manage view tokens

Separate rights are used to manage Monitor tokens:

  • Edit Tokens — allows you to create and edit monitoring tokens and location sharing links.

  • Delete Tokens — allows you to delete monitoring tokens.

For a regular user to be able to create, edit, or delete a link in the PILOT web version, an administrator or master must grant them the right to edit and delete tokens.

How to grant rights to a user

  • In “Contract settings”, open the “Staff and groups” tab

2. Double-click the user in the list to open their card

3. Go to the “Rights” tab

4. Expand the “Tokens” group

5. Select the required rights:

  • Edit Tokens — to create and edit tokens

  • Delete Tokens — to delete tokens

6. Click “Save”

How to create a view token

  • In the “Monitor tokens” section, click the “Add token” button

    2. In the window that opens, fill in the token information:

  • Specify the validity period — select the date and time when the token starts and stops working

  • Select which map to use to display the objects

  • Specify whether to display object markers or sensors on the map

  • From the list, select the objects to track with this token

    3. Click “Save”

    4. The system creates a unique link or an iframe — an embed code

    5. Copy the link or code and send it to whoever needs access to the information

Access token

This type of token is used to sign in to the system without a password. When you follow the special link, PILOT signs you in as the user, the same way as with a login and password. A token can have a limited validity period or be unlimited.

How to create an access token

  • In the “Access tokens” section, click the “Add token” button

  • In the new window, specify the date and time when the token starts and stops being valid. If you do not specify an end, the token works indefinitely.

  • Click “Save”

To edit a token, click the pencil icon , and to delete it, click the trash can icon .

The buttons for exporting and uploading display settings templates are available on any tab of “Contract settings”.

Exporting a template

2. Click the “Download settings” icon

3. Select the checkboxes for the parameters to include in the template

4. Click “Export”

The object card stores information about the vehicle and the settings of the hardware associated with it. Here you can change the main characteristics of the object, configure the device and its connection, add SIM cards, add fuel parameters, and other data.

To open the object card, double-click the object in the list, or open the object's context menu and select “Edit”.

The card has several tabs:

  • “Main” — vehicle information, its image, the device, and connection parameters

  • “SIM cards” — slot numbers, MSISDN, ICCID, and carriers of the SIM cards of the main and additional devices

  • “Info” — additional information about the object

  • “Settings” — operating and display parameters of the object

  • “Additional parameters” — additional characteristics and settings

  • “Fuel” — parameters related to fuel accounting

  • “Files” — documents and other files of the object

The “Main” tab contains information about the vehicle and the parameters of the connected hardware.

To add an object, fill in the required fields. You can add the remaining data right away or later when editing the card.

  • mileage — if its value is configured on the “Info” tab

  • engine hours — if their value is configured on the “Info” tab

  • the object image — the standard image of the selected make, model, and modification, or a photo you uploaded

Object information

Vehicle number

Enter the number or a descriptive name for the object. It is displayed in the object list, on the map, and in reports.

Vehicle type and color

Select the vehicle type, for example a passenger car, a truck, or special equipment. The system uses the corresponding icon in the object list and on the map. Next to it you can select the color used to display it.

Group

Select the folder where the object is placed in the object tree. Creating and configuring groups is described in the article “Object list”.

Make

Select the vehicle manufacturer.

Model

Select a model from the list. The list of available models depends on the selected make.

Modification

If necessary, select a specific version of the model, for example a variant with a particular body type, engine, or year of manufacture.

After you select the make and model, the system automatically adds the standard image of the vehicle.

Template

Select a ready-made set of settings for the object, for example a sensor template or an eco-driving template. Use the template that matches the installed hardware and the purpose of the vehicle.

Description

Add information that may be needed when working with the object: department, purpose, operating specifics, or other additional information.

Device tags

Assign tags for additional classification and quick search of objects. Creating tags is described in the article “Object tags”.

Object photo

On the “Main” tab you can add a photo of the vehicle:

1. Click the camera icon next to the image

2. Select a file on your computer and upload the photo

3. Turn on the toggle next to the photo if you want to show it instead of the standard vehicle icon

The photo is displayed in the object list and on the map. If the toggle is off, the system keeps using the standard icon of the selected vehicle type.

To delete the uploaded photo, click the trash can icon next to the image.

Device and connection

This block configures the main telematics hardware of the object.

Device type

Select the model of the GPS tracker or other terminal installed on the vehicle. The selected type determines how incoming data is processed and the connection parameters.

If the model you need is not in the list, contact technical support.

Device ID/IMEI

Enter the unique identifier of the main terminal. It can be an ID, a serial number, or an IMEI — it is usually printed on the device body, the packaging, or in the manufacturer's documentation.

PILOT uses this value to determine which object the incoming data belongs to.

A lock icon is displayed next to the “Device ID/IMEI” field. It protects the identifier from accidental changes. To edit the value, click the lock — the field becomes available for input.

Additional devices

You can link other installed hardware to the object, for example an additional tracker or a video device:

1. Click the edit icon in the “Additional devices” (Additional Devices) field

2. In the window that opens, click “Add”

3. Enter the IMEI — the unique identifier of the additional device

4. Select the device type

5. Click “Save”

The additional device settings include service parameters:

  • Ignore Coord — do not use the additional device's coordinates to determine the object's position

  • Ignore Retrans — do not forward the additional device's data through the configured retransmission channels

Enable these parameters only if the connection scheme requires it. If you are not sure about the setting, contact your administrator or technical support.

Server and port

After you select the device type, PILOT automatically shows the server address and port the terminal must send data to.

Click the copy icon next to the field to copy the value and use it when configuring the hardware. The field is filled in by the system and cannot be edited manually.

Time zone

Select the time zone the object operates in. It is used to display time correctly in history, events, and reports.

Packet time offset

Specify the difference in hours if the device transmits time in a format other than GMT. The default value is 0. Change the offset only if the time of the device's messages differs from the actual time.

Availability of settings

The set and availability of fields depend on the user's rights. For the “User” role:

— the “Device type” field is not available for viewing

— mileage, engine hours, and packet time offset may be available for viewing only

The “Settings” tab contains parameters that the system administrator configures through special configurations. Configurations are ready-made sets or templates of settings that the administrator can apply to objects. To learn how to add an object settings configuration through the admin panel, see here.

To configure the parameters, contact the administrator, who will add the required configurations to your contract; they will then appear on the “Settings” tab of the object card.
Settings defined by a configuration are automatically applied to all objects in the contract.

The “Settings” tab defines parameters that affect how the device works in the system. For example, here you can configure the trip and parking detector, the splitting of trips into time segments, and data filtering.

1. Speed source
Select the speed source to get correct data about the vehicle's movement. GPS speed is used by default, but if necessary you can select another parameter, for example speed from the CAN bus.
If CAN speed is selected as the source, then:
  • the chart in “History” shows the speed from CAN
  • in basic reports (trips, time in motion, parking, etc.) movement is calculated from the CAN speed
  • time in motion and stops are also calculated from the CAN speed
If the selected parameter contains no speed data, the system automatically falls back to the standard GPS speed.
Make sure you select a speed parameter. If you accidentally select, for example, mileage or another indicator, the calculations may be incorrect.
In the “Speed source” block, the “Formula” field lets you set a conversion of the parameter value into a correct speed.
CAN bus speed is not always transmitted in the required units. For example, the value may arrive in knots or meters per second. In this case, the formula lets you convert the device's technical data into a form suitable for display and calculations in the system.
For example, if the speed arrives in m/s, you can use the formula: * 3.6 (conversion from m/s to km/h)
2. Trip and parking detector
With the “Trip and parking detector” function you configure:
  • The minimum speed at which the system starts registering a trip
  • The minimum time between trips that must pass between the end of one trip and the start of the next for the system to separate them
  • The minimum parking time during which the vehicle must remain stationary for the system to record it as parking
  • The maximum distance between tracking points at which the system treats them as part of the same trip
3. Ignition accounting, speed recovery, and CAN mileage
If you enable the “Ignition accounting” function, a trip is recorded only when the vehicle's ignition is on.
The “Speed recovery” function restores the driving speed if the speed data was lost or distorted.
When “CAN mileage accounting” is enabled, the trip history and reports show the mileage received from the CAN bus — the vehicle's on-board computer — rather than the mileage calculated from the GPS tracker data.  The GPS signal is sometimes lost, so mileage from the CAN bus data  is more accurate.
4. Split trips into segments by time
The “Splitting trips into time segments” function divides each trip into several parts by time. You can configure the intervals at which trips are split, for example every 2 or 4 hours. Instead of one record for the whole day, you get data for short intervals. This level of detail is useful, for example, when preparing waybills for specific periods rather than for the whole day.
5. Event filtering
With the “Event filtering” function, configure the parameters the system uses to determine the reliability of the received data.
  • Minimum number of satellites for accurate coordinates. For the device to determine accurate location coordinates, it must receive signals from at least 3 satellites. Some devices determine the location with 2 satellites, but in that case the accuracy of the coordinates is lower.
  • Maximum HDOP value. HDOP is a horizontal error indicator that characterizes the accuracy of the device's coordinates. The lower the HDOP value, the more accurate the coordinates. You can set the maximum HDOP value at which the system accepts data as reliable. If the HDOP in a message is higher than the specified value, the message is filtered out — deleted — so that inaccurate data is not used.
The system also automatically filters out messages without coordinates or with zero latitude or longitude values, even if the device did not mark them as invalid.
  • Maximum speed value. Points with a speed above this value are filtered out when building history tracks and in speed, violation, and mileage reports.
6. Formula
The “Formula” field in the track settings is intended for filtering data packets when building tracks. It is a tool that helps exclude certain data from track building based on specified conditions.
How it works:
The formula returns TRUE or FALSE for each data packet. If the result is TRUE, the packet is not used to build the track; if the result is FALSE, the packet is used to build the track.
For example, =%S%<5
In this formula, %S% is the speed parameter. The formula returns TRUE if the speed is below 5 km/h. All packets with a speed below 5 km/h are filtered out.
You can also  use more complex formulas with logical operators, parentheses, and multiple conditions. To learn how to work with formulas, see this article.
For example, =%S%<5 || %S%>200
This formula excludes from tracks the data where the speed is below 5 km/h or above 200 km/h.

The Valid flag in raw data

Valid is a field in the raw data of a packet that shows whether the packet is considered reliable for further coordinate processing.

Valid = 0 means the packet is considered unreliable. Such packets are stored in the system but are excluded from processing when tracks, geofences, and other operations that require reliable coordinates are recalculated.

The Valid = 0 mark is assigned in only two cases:

• the packet has no coordinates, or zero latitude or longitude values are transmitted

• the packet falls under the specified filtering formula

After such a packet is saved, its participation in recalculation can no longer be changed: it will not be used when the data is reprocessed.

The filters by the number of satellites, speed, and other parameters from the “Event filtering” block work differently. They are applied dynamically, only during data recalculation. If you change the parameters of these filters and run the recalculation again, the result may change.

For example, if the minimum number of satellites in the object settings is 4, packets with fewer satellites may be excluded when tracks and reports are recalculated. But the packets themselves do not get the Valid = 0 mark.

If you want such packets to be marked as unreliable right away, use a filtering formula. For example: %satsinview% < 4

This formula marks packets where the number of satellites is less than 4 as Valid = 0. These packets are stored in the system but do not participate in the recalculation of tracks, geofences, and other data.

7. Additional
  • Speed control. If the speed exceeds the specified limit, the system reports speeding.
  • Loss of connection. If the connection with the device is lost and not restored within the specified time, the system sends a connection loss message.
  • Idle. If the object does not move for the specified time, the system records this as idle.
    Next to these fields there are additional control icons:
Bell icon — controls notifications for the limit:
  — notifications are sent,  — notifications are disabled
The limit itself keeps working: the data is recorded in the system and shown in reports.
To change the mode, click the icon.
Ignition key icon (available for the “Idle” field) — determines whether the ignition state is taken into account when calculating idle time.
— idle is recorded only when the ignition is on, — idle is counted regardless of the ignition state

The object menu is a list of actions you can perform with the selected object.

To open the object menu, right-click the object in the object list.

The set of actions available in the object menu depends on the modules connected to your contract.

Let's look at the main actions you can perform with an object through the menu.

Current track

The current track shows where the object is now and how it has been moving recently. You see its location and route on the map.

1. Current route of the object
2. Movement history player
With the player you can review how the object moved: its route, speed, and travel time.
3. Follow the object on the track
Turn on the “Follow” function to watch the object's movement online.
4. Playback speed
You can increase or decrease the playback speed. 
To finish viewing the route, click the cross.

Follow object

Click the “Follow object” function — and you see its location on the map.

To cancel following, click the cross.

If you click the object icon, an information tooltip about it appears.

Map

The map is a tool for viewing objects in detail. When you use this function, a mini window with a map opens; you can move it around the screen and resize it as you like.

You can view the locations of several objects in turn. Select several objects in the list at the same time — each object is shown in close-up one after another. This way, the location of all selected objects is always available. Open mini maps are saved in the browser and are restored automatically after the page is refreshed

Edit

To change the object information, select the edit function. The object card opens, where you can make changes.

To quickly open the object card for editing, simply double-click the object in the list with the left mouse button.

Highlight with color

Highlight with color is a quick way to highlight important objects in the list so that you notice them right away.

Sensors

When you click this item of the object menu, you go to the sensor settings window. Here you can add and configure the object's sensors.

Points

The “Points” item takes you to a window with information about raw points.

Raw points are unprocessed information that sensors collect from the device in real time.

What raw points include:

  • The exact time the data was received

  • Location — latitude, longitude, altitude

  • Driving speed

  • Direction

  • Number of satellites

  • Readings of additional sensors, for example temperature, fuel level, battery charge, and pressure sensors

View the object's status data in a table or on a chart.

1 — Select the period for building the points report. In this report you can select data for only one day for one object

2 — Build the report

3 — Build a chart. Select sensors, and their values are displayed on the chart

To download the raw points data, click .

Temporary blocking

Temporary blocking is a pause mode for an object in the system. When the equipment is not in use, for example in winter, you can suspend data collection and the deduction of the subscription fee. This function suits, for example, seasonal equipment that operates only part of the year.

Clone

When you have similar objects with small differences, use cloning. It is a quick way to create a copy of an existing object.

The system automatically copies all settings, but in the card you need to enter a new name for the object and change the unique identifier.

Import WLN

This function transfers objects from the Wialon system to PILOT. To learn how to work with this function, see here.

History

When you click “History” in the object menu, you go to the “History” section, where you can view all the information about this object's past movements and status.

Delete object

When you delete an object, all its data and history disappear. If you need to restore the information, contact the system administrator.

Menu for working with several objects

  • In the object list, select several objects while holding the Ctrl key on the keyboard

2. Right-click the objects — the menu for working with several objects opens

Edit

The “Edit” button is activated only when you select objects with the same device type.

Select objects with the same device type for bulk editing.

When you click “Edit”, a window with settings for the selected objects opens. In this window you can configure parameters for all the selected objects at once.

oshibka-vremeni-v-dannykh-obekta:
PILOT checks the time in the data transmitted by the tracker. If the data is too old or contains a date from the future, a red error icon appears in the object list next to the object's status.

The object may still appear online, but new points may not appear on the map. The “Online” status shows that the tracker maintains a connection with the system. The error icon helps you understand why the incoming data does not update the object's position.

How to view the details

Click the red icon next to the object. The “Data error” window opens with the following information:

  • Current problem — the tracker transmits data that is too old or data with a date from the future

  • Last correct update — the time of the last update with a correct time

  • Error started — when the system detected the current problem

  • Last incorrect packet — the date and time specified by the tracker in the latest data with the error. This time may differ from the time the system received it.

What to do when the error appears

1. Check the date, time, and time zone in the tracker settings. Incorrect settings may cause the error

2. Check time synchronization. If the tracker receives time from GPS or GLONASS, make sure synchronization works. If the time is not updated, restart the tracker

3. If the error persists, contact the specialist who services the hardware. Give them a screenshot of the “Data error” window. The specialist will check the firmware, the data transmission settings, and the reason why old data or data with a date from the future is being sent

4. If you need help from PILOT technical support, specify the object name and the tracker ID, and attach a screenshot of the “Data error” window. The screenshot shows the type of problem and the update times

The red icon next to the object disappears automatically after data with a correct time is received. The OK button only closes the window and does not eliminate the error.

To add a sensor:

  • Open the object menu. To do this, right-click the object in the object list

2. Click the “Sensors” tab in the object menu

3. In the window that opens, on the “Sensors” tab, click the button for adding a sensor

  1. In the window that appears, select the sensor type by purpose. For example, a battery charge sensor

  1. Fill in the required fields for adding a sensor — enter the name and description, and select the field in which the device sends the values the sensor needs. Configure the necessary parameters

6. Click the “Save” button. Check that the sensor appears in the list of active sensors

To check that the sensor works correctly and transmits data:

2. Go to the “Points” tab

Sensor parameters window

When you add or edit a sensor, its parameters window opens. To open the parameters window to edit a sensor, double-click the sensor in the list.

The following fields are filled in in the sensor parameters window:

 Sensor parameter field
  Description
Purpose
When adding a sensor, select its purpose from the drop-down list
Type
Type of the sensor by its operating principle, for example two-position, pulse, or discrete. When you select the sensor purpose, the system determines the sensor type automatically
Name
This is a required field. Enter the sensor name to distinguish it in the system. For quick filling, use the icon— copy the sensor purpose. If the object has several sensors of the same type, enter a unique name
Description
This is a required field. Enter the sensor description. For quick filling, use the icon

This is a required field. From the drop-down list, select the field that shows the value for the sensor
Unit of measurement
Define the units in which the sensor values are displayed, for example: liters, kilometers
Group
Select a group for the sensor. To learn how to create a group of sensors, see here
Conversion formula
Use a formula to calculate the sensor values. A mathematical formula helps recalculate raw data and correct the sensor readings
Tags
Assign a tag to the sensor. To learn how to create a tag, see here
Minimum and maximum
value
  Set the range of valid values. This way, the sensor filters out incorrect readings
Minimum and maximum threshold
Configure the working range of the sensor — the valid value limits within which the sensor operates normally. If the readings go outside this range, the system records a deviation
On and off names
Specify the names for the “on” and “off” states

In addition to filling in the sensor parameters, you can select additional options with checkboxes.

Additional options
Description
Event filter
The event filter protects against accidental sensor triggering caused by brief interference. It sets after how many data packets or seconds the system records a change in the sensor state. It applies to on and off sensors. In the filter you can configure two parameters: the number of received data packets and the time in seconds.
For example, if you set the value 3, the system confirms turning the sensor on or off only after receiving three packets with this signal. If you set 10 seconds, the system checks whether the sensor state has changed within this period
Create events
The sensor records changes, and the system creates entries in the event log
Filter values
The function discards unreliable sensor readings. The value received from the sensor is converted by the formula and then compared with the valid range specified in the calibration table. If the value is outside the valid range, it is discarded and not taken into account.
Show in tooltips
The sensor and its values are displayed in the tooltips of the object
Fixed values
The function sets specific values at which the sensor is considered on or off. It is used when the sensor transmits fixed numbers rather than a range. Specify the known values, for example, if the sensor transmits the value = 38 when on and 37 when off, all other values are ignored.
Save history
When history is saved, sensor readings are reflected in reports. If history is not saved, only the current readings are available
Count engine hours
The system tracks the running time of the engine or equipment based on the sensor data
Show sensor value
in the app
If the option is on, the sensor value is visible in the smartphone app. If it is off, the value is not displayed in the mobile version.
  Aggregation period
  (Aggregation period)
The minimum time interval over which the sensor data is grouped (aggregated) 
into one event.
  • If off — the system takes into account every individual message from the sensor. Because of this, reports may show many short triggers, false on and off switches, and the sensor's operating intervals look “ragged” and unstable.
  • If on and set to, for example, 120 seconds — the system combines all sensor values received within this interval into one event. That is, the sensor stops “flickering” because of frequent messages and works more stably.

Additional settings for some sensors:

Number of points for detecting a threshold exceedance
In a temperature sensor, this parameter determines how many times in a row the sensor must record a threshold exceedance for the system to treat the event as real. For example, if set to 6, the system reacts only after six consecutive confirmed measurements. This helps avoid false triggers caused by brief interference.
Smoothing coefficient
The smoothing coefficient helps make the data more accurate. It removes sharp jumps in the readings, which are often erroneous
How the smoothing coefficient works:
1. The system takes several measurements before and after each measurement point
2. Removes the highest and lowest values, which may be errors
3. Calculates the average of the remaining measurements
4. Uses this average instead of the original value
You can configure the smoothing coefficient — n. It is a number that determines how many points to the left and right of each measurement on the chart are used for smoothing. The higher the coefficient, the stronger the smoothing.
For example, if n = 3, the system takes 3 points to the left and 3 to the right of each measurement. The choice of n depends on how detailed the data you need is and how strongly you want to remove fluctuations in the measurements
Working temperature range
Valid threshold values within which the temperature is considered normal
  “Active” switch
 
 
 
Turns the analysis of refuels and fuel drains by the sensor on or off.
For fuel sensors: all enabled sensors of the object are first summed to obtain the total volume of fuel in the vehicle, and only then are events searched for in the sum.
If turned off — the sensor is used as a regular one, without automatic event search.
Removal of symmetric refuels or drains
The function excludes from the report records of refuels or fuel drains with an insignificant change in fuel level. For example, if the sensor recorded a brief change in fuel level caused by a road slope or a technical failure, the system filters out these records

PILOT has two kinds of calibration tables: a calibration table with a chart and a calibration table with text states. You can edit a calibration table only after the new sensor is saved.

A calibration table is a lookup reference that converts technical sensor readings into meaningful values.

Let's look at an example of using a calibration table for a fuel level sensor.

Suppose we have a fuel tank of non-standard shape, so its volume cannot be expressed as a simple function of the fuel level.

We install a fuel level sensor in it that works on the rheostat principle. It does not measure the fuel volume directly but changes its electrical resistance depending on the liquid level. As a result, the sensor outputs data in ohms rather than liters. The sensor resistance range is 10 to 180 ohms. To determine the fuel level in the tank correctly, you need to perform calibration and create a correspondence table.

Tank calibration:

1. Empty the tank completely and record the minimum sensor resistance value

2. Then pour in fuel in portions, for example 10 liters each, and record the resistance readings

3. Record the sensor readings after each pour

4. Repeat the process until the tank is full

5. Create the calibration table – the correspondence between the fuel level in liters and the sensor resistance in ohms

Example of a calibration table for a 100-liter tank

When the sensor transmits, for example, 100 ohms, the system uses the calibration table to determine that the tank contains about 40 liters of fuel. If the sensor transmits 110 ohms, the system calculates that the fuel level is about 35 liters.

Calibration table with a chart

A type of calibration table in which sensor readings are converted to real values using a dependency chart. The X axis shows the sensor readings, and the Y axis shows the real values of the measured quantity. A chart is built between the entered points and determines the real value for a sensor reading. This type of calibration table is often used for fuel level, weight, temperature, and humidity sensors.

How to create a table

You can configure the table in the sensor parameters window or upload a ready-made one from a file. A configured table can be saved to a file and used for other similar sensors.

To open the calibration table, click “Edit”.

Edit table

How to add values to the table:

  • Click “Add”

2. Enter the real amount of fuel and the value the sensor shows

3. Click “Save”

4. Repeat the steps for all the required readings

Example of a filled-in table

Calibration table with text states

This type of calibration table is used for multi-position sensors and converts the sensor's numeric values into statuses that are easy for the user to understand.

Let's look at an example of using this type of table.

For example, we have a multi-position GPS antenna sensor that shows the signal level. A GPS receiver measures signal strength in dBm, where values are usually in the range from -160 dBm to -120 dBm.

In the table, we convert the technical values sent by the sensor into understandable statuses: “No signal”, “Weak signal”, “Medium signal”, “Good signal”.

When the sensor sends a value, for example -135 dBm, the system finds the match in the table and converts it into a text status — “Weak signal”. The text status is shown in the object's tooltip and in reports.

Such a calibration table can be used for different parameters, for example, you can set value ranges for temperature measurement: “Cold” — 0–10°C, “Warm” — 10–25°C, “Hot” — 25°C and above; or display the battery charge not as a percentage but as the statuses “Low”, “Medium”, “Full”.

How to add a calibration table for multi-position sensors:

  • Open the sensor parameters window

  • In the “Calibration table” section, click “Edit”

  • In the calibration table window, click “Add”

  • Fill in the columns with the minimum and maximum sensor values,

  • Set the text statuses in the “Semantics” column

  • Select an icon and a Background color for the status. The status color is used on charts and in history when building the track.

  • Click “Save”

In this article we look at the sensor types that exist in the PILOT system, what they are used for, and which parameters you need to configure for some of them to work correctly.

— what sensor types exist and how they work

— how to choose the sensor purpose and its type

— how to configure a fuel sensor

Sensor types

The sensor type determines which parameters it controls in the monitoring system. Let's look in more detail at which sensor types exist and what they are used for in PILOT.

When adding a sensor, first select its purpose. The type is determined automatically, but you can change it if necessary.

1 — Sensor purpose

2 — Sensor type

Sensor types by operating principle

Text sensors

Displays the device state in words.

For example, instead of technical codes, a lock sensor outputs the messages “Lock open” and “Lock closed”.

Discrete sensors

Pass on data in the form in which the device sent it. To get an exact value, this data can be converted using calibration tables or formulas.

For discrete sensors you can enable the alerts function. When the sensor state changes, the system sends notifications by e-mail or SMS.

Pulse sensors

Count the number of pulses between readings.

For example, an engine hours sensor that records the number of pulses to calculate equipment running time.

Two-position sensors

Record two states of an object: on — off or open — closed.

The system determines its state by a range of values: if the reading falls between the set minimum and maximum, the sensor is considered on, otherwise off.

Discrete integral sensors

Work on the principle of discrete sensors but additionally accumulate the received values.

For example, such a sensor can count the total number of events — how many times the engine was started or the body doors were opened during a shift.

Pulse integral sensors

An analog of pulse sensors, but with the function of accumulating the total number of pulses.

For example, such sensors can count the total number of pulses to analyze long-term equipment operation — the total engine running time over a month or the total mileage of a vehicle over a quarter.

Two-position inverse sensors

Work the same way as two-position sensors but show the state in reverse order.

For example, you need the alarm to go off when a door is opened without authorization. A regular sensor may fail to trigger because of the wiring specifics, while an inverse sensor “flips” the signal: when the door is open, the sensor shows “closed”; when it is closed, it shows “open”, to guarantee that the alarm is triggered. This way, the sensor insures the system against errors.

Multi-position sensors

Used to register readings that can take several values. The values are interpreted based on a calibration table. For example, temperature, humidity, or pressure sensors.

Composite sensors

Combine data from several sensors.

For example, combining data from a fuel sensor and an engine hours sensor to calculate fuel consumption per unit of time.

Special sensors

Such sensors are designed to collect highly specialized information.

For example, an RFID sensor can recognize objects and people, a GPS sensor determines the exact location, a CAN bus sensor collects the vehicle's technical parameters, and a people counter counts the number of visitors in a room.

How this sensor detects a refuel:
1. Refuel detection
The sensor constantly monitors the fuel level and records the readings.
  • The system takes 5 consecutive fuel level measurements
  • Compares the difference between the first and the last measurement
  • If the difference between them is greater than the specified value, the system considers it a refuel. This value is set in the sensor settings.
2. Refuel start
When the system has detected a refuel, it analyzes the data for the last 20 minutes. It looks for the measurement point with the lowest fuel level in this time span. The system considers this point the start of the refuel.
3. Refuel end
The system understands that the refuel has ended:
  • If five measurements in a row show the same fuel level — the vehicle has been refueled and is standing still
  • If the next measurement shows less fuel than the previous one — the vehicle has been refueled and started moving
  • If the signal disappears for an hour, the system considers that the vehicle's power was cut off, for example the ignition was turned off, which can also mean the end of the refuel
A fuel drain is detected the same way as a refuel, except that instead of an increase in the fuel level the system records a sharp decrease.
The system detects a refuel or fuel drain by comparing the fuel level at several points. If data arrives too often, increase the number of points in the sensor settings to avoid false triggers. If too rarely, decrease it.
Rotation speed
  Discrete
Measures the number of revolutions of the engine or other rotating mechanisms. It is used, for example, to monitor the rotation speed of the engine, a concrete mixer drum, or other equipment. The measurement result is shown in revolutions per minute — RPM
Engine hours sensor
  Discrete
Reads the number of pulses between readings to record equipment running time. It is used to account for the running time of the engine or other devices
Concrete mixer loading or unloading sensor
  Two-position
Used to track the loading and unloading of materials in construction machinery
RFID reader
  Special
Used to read RFID tags and recognize objects or users.
An RFID tag is an electronic tag or chip that stores a unique code for identifying an object or a person. It works as a contactless electronic pass
Humidity sensor
  Discrete
Used to monitor the humidity level, for example in refrigeration units, warehouses, and other places where it is important to maintain the required humidity. It shows just a number, for example 60%, or an acceptable humidity range, for example, normal is 40-60%
Weight sensor
  Discrete
Used to measure the load on a vehicle

  Text
Sends the password to unlock the lock. After it triggers, a new item appears in the object menu — “Open lock”

  Two-position
Sends a signal that the device is switching to sleep mode. When it is time to go to sleep mode, the device sends a last message with  an event number and then stops transmitting data completely
Security sensor
  Two-position
Can be in two states: “on” or “off”. For example, such a sensor monitors the opening of a door or window in case of a possible intrusion
Battery connection
  Two-position
Determines whether the battery is connected or not
 
Relative odometer
 
   Pulse
A sensor for calculating mileage from the speedometer or other connected equipment data. It accounts for the distance traveled when GPS/GLONASS data is missing or not accurate enough.
The terminal counts pulses between message transmissions, and PILOT sums the received values and converts them into distance.
To configure it, specify the number of pulses per kilometer. The value is determined separately for each vehicle because it depends on the installed equipment. For example, if 1000 pulses correspond to one kilometer, enter 1000 in the “Pulses per kilometer” field
nastrojka-datchika-topliva:
The fuel sensor in the system has many parameters. Here we look at how to configure it correctly to get accurate data and record refuel and fuel drain events properly.

General sensor settings

  • Purpose — the sensor type in the system

  • Type — the sensor's operating principle, for example “Discrete”

  • Name — the internal name of the sensor shown in the interface

  • Field — the hardware input of the tracker the sensor is connected to

  • Description — additional information about the sensor

  • Units of measurement — usually liters (“l.”)

  • Conversion formula — if you need to correct the data

  • Tags — labels for convenient search and filtering of sensors

Detecting refuels and fuel drains

To determine refuels and fuel drains correctly, the filtering parameters and trigger thresholds must be configured properly in the system. This helps exclude false events and improve data accuracy.

  • The “Active” switch — turns the analysis of refuels and fuel drains by this sensor on or off.

    For fuel sensors: all enabled sensors of the object are first summed to obtain the total volume of fuel in the vehicle, and only then are events searched for in the sum. If turned off, the sensor works as a regular one, without searching for refuels and fuel drains.

Drain through the return line

The “Drain through the return line” function helps detect hidden theft through the return line — the fuel line through which unused fuel returns to the tank.

After the function is enabled, the system analyzes abnormal fuel consumption while driving, calculates the volume of a possible drain, and marks the place of the event on the map.

Trigger thresholds

  • Refuel threshold — the minimum increase in fuel level that the system considers a refuel

  • Fuel drain threshold — the minimum decrease in fuel level that is recorded as a fuel drain

These parameters help to:

— ignore minor fluctuations in fuel level

— exclude sensor noise

— record only real events

Driving speed filter

The speed filter is used to exclude false events while driving.

For example:

— fuel consumption on the road is not detected as a fuel drain

— fluctuations in fuel level are not counted as a refuel

The system analyzes the object's speed at the time of the event and, depending on the selected mode, can ignore points with high speed.

  • Maximum speed for detection (event search) — the speed in km/h below which the vehicle is considered stationary

  • Speed mode — how exactly to check the speed within an event

    Speed accounting mode options:

  • All points — all points of the event must be below the set speed threshold

  • Start — it is enough for only the first point of the event to be below the speed threshold

  • Any point — the event is counted if at least one point meets the condition (for example, is in parking)

  • Average speed — the system compares the average speed of the event with the set threshold

  • Off — disables the speed check. In this mode, refuels and fuel drains are recorded regardless of speed

  • Coefficient — checks whether enough points have a speed below the threshold. It fine-tunes the filtering with additional parameters:

— Minimum share of slow points — defines the percentage of event points that must be at low speed. For example: a value of 0.5 means at least 50%

— Minimum parking duration — sets the total time during which the object must be at low speed

This mode handles situations where the beginning of a refuel or its “tail” falls on a short stretch of movement, but the vehicle was actually stationary most of the time

Fuel change rate filter

These parameters let you distinguish real events from natural fuel consumption.

  • Minimum refuel rate — the minimum rate of fuel level increase (l/h) for an event to be considered a refuel. If the fuel level rises too slowly, the event is not considered a refuel.

  • Minimum fuel drain rate — the minimum level drop (l/h) for an event to be considered a fuel drain. If the fuel decreases more slowly than the set value, the event is ignored.

Sensitivity to sensor noise

  • Smoothing coefficient — the degree of chart smoothing before analysis. It is used when there is noise in the fuel sensor data.

    The higher the value, the smoother the chart and the fewer sharp jumps, which are often caused by sensor errors.

Removal of symmetric events

This function helps exclude from the report false operations in which a refuel and a fuel drain occur with almost identical volumes (for example, a road slope or a technical failure).

  • The “Remove symmetric refuels/drains” switch — enables the search for “drain → refuel” or “refuel → drain” pairs with very close volumes

  • Maximum difference, % — the allowed difference in the pair's volumes in percent

  • Maximum difference, l — how much the volumes in liters may differ.

  • Maximum distance (interval between events), h — the time span within which events are considered a “pair”, for example 12 hours.

Watch the YouTube video that shows how to set up the refuel and fuel drain detector.

The “Relative odometer” sensor calculates the object's mileage from the number of pulses transmitted by the terminal. It suits hardware that counts pulses before sending a data packet and starts a new count after sending.

PILOT adds up the values from the received messages and converts them to kilometers. The “Pulses per kilometer” coefficient is used for the calculation.

Configure the sensor separately for each object: the number of pulses per kilometer depends on the vehicle and the installed hardware.

Before setting up, make sure that:

— the terminal transmits the number of pulses in a separate field

— each value contains the number of pulses counted since the previous packet was sent

— the number of pulses corresponding to one kilometer of travel is known

If the terminal transmits a constantly increasing total counter, the “Relative odometer” sensor with the “Pulse” type is not suitable for such data.

How to add the sensor

  • Add a new sensor to the object

    3. In the “Purpose” field, select “Relative odometer”.

    4. Make sure the “Type” field is set to “Pulse”

    5. In the “Name” field, enter a descriptive name for the sensor, for example “Relative odometer”

    6. In the “Field” field, specify the parameter in which the terminal transmits the number of pulses

    7. If necessary, fill in the “Conversion formula”. If the terminal transmits a ready number of pulses and no additional conversion is required, leave the field empty

    8. In the “Pulses per kilometer” field, enter the number of pulses corresponding to one kilometer of travel

9. If necessary, turn on “Filter values” to exclude incorrect readings

10. Click “Save”

After saving, PILOT starts adding up the values from the selected field and calculating mileage using the specified number of pulses per kilometer.

Calculating mileage from pulses

A pulse is a signal the terminal receives from connected equipment while the vehicle is moving. The greater the distance the vehicle covers, the more pulses the terminal records.

In each packet, the terminal transmits the number of pulses accumulated since the previous packet was sent. PILOT adds up these values for the selected period and calculates mileage with the formula: Mileage, km = sum of pulses ÷ number of pulses per kilometer

For example, the sensor settings specify 1000 pulses per kilometer. During a trip, the terminal transmitted three values: 200, 350, and 450.

First, PILOT adds up the pulses: 200 + 350 + 450 = 1000 pulses

Then it calculates the mileage: 1000 ÷ 1000 = 1 km

The value in the “Pulses per kilometer” field must be greater than zero. The more accurately the coefficient is specified, the more accurately the mileage is calculated.

How to determine the number of pulses per kilometer

If the coefficient is unknown, determine it with a test trip:

1. Record the initial mileage and pulse counter readings

2. Drive a test distance. For a more accurate result, it is better to choose a long enough section, for example 10 kilometers

3. Determine the total number of pulses received during the trip

4. Divide the number of pulses by the distance traveled: Pulses per kilometer = number of pulses ÷ distance, km

For example, over 10 kilometers the terminal transmitted 12,500 pulses: 12,500 ÷ 10 = 1250 pulses per kilometer

Enter 1250 in the “Pulses per kilometer” field.

After calibration, make another test trip and compare the calculated mileage with the actual one. If the values differ, refine the coefficient.

Checking the calculation

Compare the calculated mileage with the vehicle's actual mileage on the test section.

If the values differ:

— check whether the field with the number of pulses is selected correctly

— make sure the terminal starts a new count after sending each packet

— adjust the “Pulses per kilometer” value

— check the completeness of the received data

If some packets did not reach PILOT, the calculated mileage may be lower than the actual one.
